questions.q: What is the technical architecture document's (TAD) primary job, per this lesson?
options: To assemble all prior deliverables into one coherent narrative, with connective prose explaining how each piece relates to the others
To introduce entirely new design content not covered in earlier deliverables
To replace the implementation roadmap with a simpler summary
To serve only as a cover page for the other deliverables
questions.explain: The TAD's entire value is in connecting already-produced deliverables into a coherent whole — nothing genuinely new should be introduced in it.

questions.q: Why should the executive summary be written last, after every other TAD section is finished?
options: Because executive summaries are legally required to be written last
Because the executive summary is the least important section
Because you can't summarize a document you haven't finished yet, and writing it last is the only reliable way to know what actually needs to be in it
Because the risk register must be finalized before any other section can be drafted
questions.explain: The lesson gives a practical reason: summarizing requires knowing what the full document actually contains, which is only certain once every other section is complete.

questions.q: Why must the TAD's executive summary stand completely on its own, independent of the rest of the document?
options: Because it's the only section that will be translated into other languages
Because many readers (a CFO, a CIO, a board member skimming before a meeting) will never read the other sections, so it has to make sense without them
Because the executive summary is the only section allowed to contain diagrams
Because it replaces the need for Lesson 1's elevator statement
questions.explain: Busy executives often read only the executive summary; if it requires the rest of the document to make sense, it has failed at its one job.

questions.q: What problem does this lesson identify with simply pasting each existing deliverable under a heading to assemble the TAD?
options: It would make the document too short to be useful
It would require rewriting the risk register from scratch
It would violate Salesforce's documentation standards
It produces a document that reads like disconnected chapters, missing the connective prose that explains how one decision necessitates another
questions.explain: Pasting deliverables under headings without connective prose leaves the reader to infer relationships (like how the single-org decision shapes the security design) themselves — the actual work of a TAD is making those connections explicit.

questions.q: According to the TAD's standard structure for LTV Global, where does the implementation roadmap appear?
options: As its own final section, following the risks and decisions section
In the executive summary only
It is omitted from the TAD entirely
Embedded only within the nonfunctional requirements section
questions.explain: The roadmap (Lesson 26) is listed as its own standard TAD section, following current state, requirements, target architecture, nonfunctional requirements, delivery strategy, and risks/decisions.
